overview.description: KarnÃ¶ffel is arguably the oldest identifiable European card game still played today, with records dating back to 1426. It is a highly unusual trick-taking game where players are allowed to communicate freely with their partners. The game is famous for its chaotic 'Elected Suit' ranking, featuring cards with evocative names like the Joker-like 'KarnÃ¶ffel' (Unter), the 'Pope' (6), and the 'Devil' (7).
overview.deck: 32 cards (Standard 32, German suits); 48-card variant also played historically.

history.origins: First mentions appear in a municipal ordinance in NÃ¶rdlingen in 1426. The name likely refers to 'testicular swelling' or 'hernia', used as a slang term for a coarse or powerful card.
timeline: 1426: Earliest written record of the game.
1500s: Becomes a symbol of social upheaval; the 'Devil' card (7) was seen as scandalous for being able to beat high cards.
1800s: Becomes a traditional folk game in rural Swiss and German regions (as KnÃ¼ffeln).
Present: Played by enthusiasts and historical reconstructionists.
history.evolution: KarnÃ¶ffel predates the concept of a 'Trump' suit as we know it today; its 'Elected Suit' has only partial trumping powers, representing a transitional phase in card game history.
history.cultural: The game was famously criticized by medieval theologians for its 'lawless' nature and for allowing low-born cards (like the 6 or 7) to defeat Kings and Emperors.

setup.deck: 32 cards (Standard 32, German suits: Acorns, Leaves, Hearts, Bells). French equivalent: remove 2s through 6s.
setup.dealing: Deal 5 cards to each player, one at a time. The first card of each player's hand is dealt face up; the lowest of these face-up cards determines the chosen (trump) suit. If two tie, the first dealt decides. Then players pick up their cards.

rules.objective: Win at least three out of the five tricks in a hand to score points for your team.
rules.gameplay:
1. Standard trick-taking. NO OBLIGATION to follow suit (this is a key medieval rule).
2. Players can talk to their partners, showing cards or suggesting plays.
3. The leader of a partnership (the Director) often makes the final decision on signals.
keyRules: No requirement to follow suit; highest card of led suit or highest trump wins the trick.
Lowest of the four face-up cards (one per player) determines the chosen (trump) suit for the deal.
First team to win three tricks wins the deal. Partners sit opposite; communication between partners is allowed.
Devil (7 of chosen suit) may not be played to the first trick; it beats all only when led.

strategy.basic: Talk! Communication is legal. Coordinate with your partner to ensure you don't 'waste' a KarnÃ¶ffel (Unter) on a trick your partner can win with a 4 or 5.
strategy.intermediate: The 'Devil' Lead: Use the Seven of the elected suit to Lead a trick you MUST win. It is almost unbeatable on the lead, but garbage if held back.
strategy.advanced: Managing the 'King-beaters': Since the 4 and 5 of trumps can only beat Kings (and lower), use them specifically when you know an opponent is holding a high card but no Master trumps.
tips: Because you don't have to follow suit, you can 'hide' your master cards until the very last trick to secure the win.
The Seven (Devil) cannot be led on the first trick in many house rules; check before playing.

difficulty.easy: Follows traditional follow-suit logic (which is unnecessary); fails to lead the Devil effectively.
difficulty.medium: Communicates basic card values to partner; understands King-beater hierarchy.
difficulty.hard: Expert at partner coordination; masters the 'Devil' lead timing; perfectly exploits the 'No Follow Suit' rule for maximum deception.

edgeCases.text: The Devil (7 of chosen suit) may not be played to the first trick.
The Devil beats all cards only when led to a trick; when played to a trick led by another, it counts only as a 7.
First team to win three tricks wins the deal. Player who led to the first trick becomes the next dealer.

engine.handRankingSystem: Trick-taking with custom elected-suit ranking: Karnöffel (Unter) beats all; Devil (7) beats all only when led; Pope (6), then King-beaters (3,4,5) in chosen suit. No obligation to follow suit. Highest of led suit or highest trump wins trick.
engine.deckDescription: A stripped French deck containing 32 cards with four suits (Hearts, Diamonds, Clubs, Spades) and eight ranks per suit (7 through Ace), created by removing all 2s through 6s from a standard 52-card deck.
engine.suitDescription: Four traditional French suits: Hearts (Cœur), Diamonds (Carreau), Clubs (Trèfle), and Spades (Pique), each represented with standard French card iconography and distinct color coding for easy recognition during gameplay.
engine.rankDescription: Eight ranks per suit in ascending order: 7, 8, 9, 10, Jack (Valet), Queen (Dame), King (Roi), and Ace as the highest card, where each rank determines card strength and eligibility for building sequences.
